title: Time Synchronization: chrony and Why Clocks Matter
intro: TLS certificates, Kerberos, JWT tokens, TOTP two-factor codes, distributed databases, and log correlation all assume clocks agree to within seconds, or less. A server whose clock drifts produces some of the strangest-looking failures in operations. chrony is the standard time daemon on modern Linux.

steps.prompt: Show the system's time settings and whether it's synchronized.
steps.fake_output:
Local time: Sun 2026-09-28 10:52:11 UTC
           Universal time: Sun 2026-09-28 10:52:11 UTC
                Time zone: Etc/UTC (UTC, +0000)
System clock synchronized: yes
              NTP service: active
steps.why: Run servers in UTC. Local time zones make log correlation across regions painful and create daylight-saving bugs twice a year. 'System clock synchronized: no' should be an alert.

steps.prompt: Show chrony's view of how far off the clock is.
steps.fake_output:
Reference ID    : A9FEA97B (169.254.169.123)
Stratum         : 4
System time     : 0.000012345 seconds fast of NTP time
Last offset     : +0.000003118 seconds
RMS offset      : 0.000021004 seconds
Leap status     : Normal
steps.explanation: 12 microseconds fast, synced to 169.254.169.123, the AWS Time Sync Service.
steps.why: Cloud providers offer local, highly accurate time sources (AWS 169.254.169.123, Google metadata.google.internal, the Azure host). Use them instead of public pool servers: they're lower latency and don't depend on internet egress.

steps.prompt: List the time sources chrony uses, with details.
steps.explanation: The AWS source is selected (*); the public pool is a backup.
steps.why: Reach 377 (octal) means the last 8 polls all succeeded. A source stuck at Reach 0 means it can't be reached: often UDP port 123 blocked by a firewall, the classic cause of drift that begins after a 'firewall hardening' change.

steps.prompt: On a VM that was paused for hours and is now 4 minutes behind, correct the clock immediately instead of slewing slowly.
steps.explanation: The clock jumped to the correct time.
steps.why: Normally chrony slews (speeds up or slows the clock gradually) so time never goes backwards, which some applications can't handle. For a large offset, slewing would take hours, so makestep jumps it once. Configure 'makestep 1 3' so this happens automatically at boot.
